analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare negotiate drug prices, taxes large price hikes, allows importing cheaper Canadian drugs, and caps monthly drug copays at $250.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in September 2018 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it died without a hearing or a vote before Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The Affordable Medications Act was a sweeping prescription drug bill. It would have required drug makers to publicly report what they spend on research, marketing, and executive pay; let Medicare negotiate prices directly with manufacturers and fall back to the lower Veterans Affairs price if talks fail; tax companies whose prices rise faster than medical inflation; let Americans import lower-priced drugs from certified Canadian pharmacies; require manufacturers to pay Medicaid-style rebates on drugs used by low-income Medicare enrollees; and cap prescription drug cost-sharing at $250 per person per month in most insurance plans.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries and other people who pay out of pocket for prescription drugs. Medicare would gain negotiating power and low-income enrollees would get manufacturer rebates, taxpayers and patients would share savings from negotiation and importation, and a $250 monthly cap would protect people on expensive medications from runaway cost-sharing.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals Medicare's 'noninterference' clause and requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate Part D drug prices, falling back to the lower Veterans Affairs price if negotiation fails after one year [S3].
Caps prescription drug cost-sharing at $250 per person per month ($500 per family) in individual and group health plans starting in 2020, adjusted for inflation afterward [S3].

Imposes an excise tax on price spikes equal to 50-100% of the revenue from increases above medical inflation, with the revenue directed toward NIH research and reducing patient cost-sharing and premiums [S3].

Requires the Secretary to allow importation of qualifying prescription drugs from certified Canadian pharmacies and wholesalers within 180 days, including for individuals up to a 90-day personal supply [S3].

Requires manufacturers to report annually on research costs, marketing and advertising, profits, executive pay, patient assistance programs, and federal benefits received, with reports made publicly available and civil penalties up to $200,000 per day for noncompliance [S3].

Requires manufacturers that want their drugs covered in Medicare Part D to pay rebates, pegged to Medicaid rebate levels, on drugs dispensed to low-income enrollees, with the rebates deposited into the Medicare trust fund [S3].
Establishes a $2 billion prize fund over ten years for new antibiotics and rewards public funding of clinical trials, aiming to spur innovation outside the high-price model [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, which would face Medicare price negotiation, an excise tax on price spikes above medical inflation, Medicaid-level rebates for low-income Medicare enrollees, public reporting of costs and profits, competition from imported drugs, and the loss of the tax deduction for direct-to-consumer drug advertising. Taxpayers would fund the $2 billion antibiotic prize fund, and drug makers argued that negotiation and price caps could reduce returns that finance research into new medicines.

drawbacks.text: The bill would impose heavy compliance costs on manufacturers: annual public reporting of itemized R&D, cost-of-goods, marketing, and executive compensation for every drug, plus quarterly reporting to the Inspector General for the price-spike tax, with penalties up to $200,000 per day [S3].

The price-spike excise tax and Medicare price negotiations could reduce manufacturer revenue on high-priced drugs, which industry contends would mean less money available for developing new medicines; the bill's own prize fund and public trial funding are a partial, but only partial, answer to that objection [S3].

The $2 billion Antibiotics Prize Fund is an outright appropriation, a real cost to taxpayers, and the drug importation program would require new certification, testing, and enforcement machinery whose safety critics and potential costs the bill attempts to manage but cannot guarantee [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to patients and Medicare are large and direct: negotiated prices, a hard monthly cap on drug cost-sharing, rebates for low-income enrollees, and access to lower-priced imported drugs. The main honest cost is that some manufacturer revenue would shrink, with a possible chilling effect on investment in marginal new drugs — the bill tries to offset that with public prizes and trial funding, an approach that addresses antibiotics but not the broader innovation question. On balance the bill's benefits to people who take prescription drugs substantially outweigh its acknowledged design costs and uncertainties.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate, sent to the Finance Committee, and sat there without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. Tina Smith introduced the Affordable Medications Act on September 5, 2018, joined by 14 cosponsors (13 Democrats and 1 Independent) [S1].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day; the full action history shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote [S5].
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, so the bill expired in committee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers are better off because the bill never advanced: Medicare price negotiation, the price-spike excise tax, Medicaid-level rebates for low-income Medicare enrollees, drug importation, and public cost-and-profit reporting all died with it, and patients and Medicare paid the prices in place instead.

for.name: Sen. Tina Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 14 cosponsors

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (13 Democrats and 1 Independent), including Sens. Sanders, Warren, Brown, and Klobuchar

against.name: Senate Finance Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on September 5, 2018 and took no further action on it — no hearing, markup, or vote — before the Congress ended

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for floor action in the remaining months of the 115th Congress

sides.party_line_note: All 15 sponsors were Democrats or independents; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill died in a committee chaired by Republicans with no recorded bipartisan support.

industries.note: The bill hits them on nearly every front: Medicare price negotiation with a VA-price fallback, an excise tax of 50-100% on price-spike revenue, Medicaid-level rebates for low-income Medicare enrollees, public reporting of R&D, marketing, and profits, importation competition, and loss of the advertising tax deduction. Their gain from the bill's death was keeping the existing pricing system intact.

industries.industry: Direct-to-consumer drug advertising (media and ad industry)
industries.note: The bill disallows the tax deduction for prescription drug advertising, raising the after-tax cost of the consumer drug-ad business that funnels demand toward high-priced brands.

Provisions on preserving access to affordable generics, tightening the 180-day exclusivity rules, and authorizing certified Canadian pharmacies and wholesalers to sell into the U.S. market would open new revenue while lowering prices for patients.
Manufacturers would have to disclose the net prices realized by PBMs after rebates, exposing the rebate intermediation that inflates list prices; PBMs' opaque margin business would face new scrutiny.
